en: Compiled by Shi Jizang. Chapter 20:
Cause and Effect (Nine Manuscripts). Chapter Twenty: Cause and Effect. Question:
Since the preceding chapters have already refuted cause and effect item by item, why is this explained again now? Answer:
Causality is the great pillar of all meanings and the very foundation for establishing correct belief;
yet those who are deluded err frequently regarding it.
Although the preceding section has briefly refuted these errors, it is necessary to discuss them again in the following section.
As the heterodox teachers posit four different schools regarding false causes and false effects, and as the ten masters of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna have various explanations,
we know that cause and effect are difficult to clarify and must be examined with great care.
Second, although the preceding sections have refuted cause and effect in order to establish other doctrines— for instance,
the "Refutation of the Four Conditions" chapter refutes the causality of the four conditions to establish the meaning of non-arising,

and even the "Refutation of the Five Aggregates" chapter refutes cause and effect to establish the meaning of the non-existence of the five aggregates— [the present section serves a different purpose].
The cause and effect have not yet been correctly discussed;
now, wishing to correctly discuss cause and effect,
this chapter has come forth.
If one follows those who have recently arrived [at this teaching], they arise from the category of time.
An opponent says:
"Since the three periods of time do not exist, how can there be the phenomena of cause and effect?"
Furthermore, the principle of cause and effect cannot be rendered non-existent;
therefore, time must exist.
Question: How many kinds of causes and effects are there?
The answer is briefly threefold. First,
cause and effect as characterized by arising,
such as a clay jar and its like.
Second is the cause and effect of the conditioned characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*),
such as the case of rolling one's fingers.
Third is the cause and effect of the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*).
Just as a lamp illuminates objects, so do the myriad practices emerge from the Dharmakāya.
Question: Does this chapter refute cause and effect, or does it expound upon cause and effect?
Answer: Within each section, there are both expositions and refutations of two meanings.
Seeking the internal or external, the great or small, the nature or reality, and cause or effect, none are found to have an origin.
Therefore, it is called "Refuting Cause and Effect."
Because those who maintain that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is real immediately subvert the principle of cause and effect,
the Master of the Treatise must refute them.
Second, only when the notion of a real intrinsic nature in cause and effect is eliminated can one properly discern the causal relationship of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Since it is called "dependent origination," cause and effect are clearly manifest yet eternally quiescent; therefore,
when one gives rise to contemplation within the causal stage, all conceptual proliferation is forgotten.
This chapter is divided into two parts:
first, the specific refutation of the ten schools' theories of cause and effect;
second, the general refutation of all theories of cause and effect.
The analysis of the ten causes and effects consists of ten sections,
which may also be grouped into five pairs.
The first is the pair of existence and non-existence.
The second is the pair of "giving" and "not giving," also called "extinguished" and "unextinguished.
The third is the pair of "simultaneous" and "sequential."
The fourth pair consists of "ceasing transformation" and "non-ceasing transformation.
The fifth pair consists of "pervasive" and "non-pervasive.
Regarding the first pair, "existence" and "non-existence," there are four verses in total.
This constitutes four distinct points.
The first verse clarifies that if the effect already exists within the cause, why would it depend on conditions to arise?
The second verse addresses how conditions could possibly produce an effect that does not exist within the cause.
The third verse further refutes the existence of an effect:
if the effect were present within the cause, it would be complete with the four sense-objects,
and thus the various sense-faculties would be able to apprehend it.
The fourth section refutes non-existence.
If the effect does not exist within the cause, then the cause is equivalent to a non-cause.
The reason for employing these four verses in an interwoven manner to refute [the opponent's position] is as follows:
Having finished refuting existence, one then clings to non-existence externally; therefore, non-existence is refuted.
Next, having finished refuting non-existence, one turns back to the fundamental tenet and clings to existence;
therefore, existence is refuted once more.
Having exhausted the refutation of existence, one proceeds to grasp non-existence;
because that which is clung to is not fixed, it is refuted through a web of interlocking arguments.
Furthermore, this treatise employs many methods of refutation.
Above, the various categories were treated according to existence and non-existence;
now, existence and non-existence are interwoven.
Because the conditions encountered differ, there are not just one, but many gates of refutation.
Question: For what reason, among the ten propositions, are existence and non-existence refuted first?
Answer: Existence and non-existence are the root of the views of annihilationism and eternalism;
annihilationism and eternalism are the foundation of all [wrong] views.
Now, because one wishes to exhaustively investigate its root, it is refuted first.
Furthermore, the causality of the Buddha-dharma is precisely the Middle Way;
existence and non-existence are direct obstructions to the Middle Way.
Furthermore, Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika are the primary systems of the non-Buddhists,
while the Sthavira and Mahāsāṃghika schools serve as the foundations for all Buddhist sects;
thus, both within and outside [the Buddhist fold], there are correct adherents to the views of existence and non-existence.
Therefore, it was refuted previously.
Question: Why were "both existence and non-existence" and "neither existence nor non-existence" not refuted?
Answer: "Existence" and "not non-existent" both still carry the meaning of existence.
Furthermore, "neither being nor non-being" is likewise synonymous with "non-existence.
Therefore, by merely refuting these two positions, the four schools are subsumed.
First, the prose section establishes [the position].
The following verse refutes this;
that is, it refutes the Sāṃkhya and the Sthavira’s assertion of the existence of the effect within the cause,
which maintains three points regarding the existence of the effect.
First, because we directly perceive that the fruit arises from causes, there is the fruit within the cause.
Second, because it arises through the conjunction of conditions,
we know that the fruit exists within the conditions.
If the conditions are not present, even if they were to combine, production would not occur.
Third is to have faith in the Buddha’s words,
as it is said in a sutra:
Because there is the nature of arising, arising is able to produce.
The first half of the verse restates [the opponent's position], while the second half refutes it.
The externalist offers this defense:
The effect does not exist within the cause;
rather, it arises through the conjunction of conditions.
Why, then, do you raise the objection that the effect need not arise from the conjunction of conditions?
Answer: To say that there is no functional entity (*vastu*) within the cause means, in the end, that there is no fruit within the cause.
Since a functional entity arises from within a cause where no such entity previously existed, one should know that this entity was originally non-existent and has now come into being.
Therefore, the effect does not exist within the causes.
Furthermore, if an event arises through the convergence of conditions, it would likewise have to be produced by their conjunction;
if this principle were self-existent, the event itself would also have to be so.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon depends upon a principle, that principle ought in turn to have something upon which it depends.
Moreover, if a phenomenon depends upon a principle, the phenomenon may be said to exist;
yet if the principle itself has no cause, then there can be no such thing as a principle.
He asked again:
"Does existence already exist fundamentally and then require the convergence of conditions,
or does it come into being only after the convergence of conditions?"
If it already exists fundamentally, what need is there for the convergence of conditions?
If it exists only after the convergence of conditions, then it is non-existent prior to that convergence.
Thus, even with the aid of the convergence of conditions, the fruit will ultimately not arise.
Question: The principle that the effect does not exist within the cause established below is precisely the Vātsīputrīya-Saṃmitīya doctrine of non-existence in the two periods [of past and future].
Answer: The first half of the verse restates [the opponent's position], while the second half refutes it.
The refutation states:
If the effect does not exist within the cause, this non-existence is no different from that of empty space or a rabbit’s horns.
Empty space and a rabbit’s horns do not arise even when conditions converge.
The fruit is also like this.
The fruit may follow that which can produce it;
however, the great void does not produce the great void, and thus the great void may be non-existent.
The effect should not be non-existent.
If both [cause and conditions] were non-existent yet the effect were produced while the great void was not,
then conversely, the great void should be produced while the effect is not.
The first half of the third verse reiterates the existence [of the pot],
while the second half refutes it directly.
According to the non-Buddhists, a pot made of clay possesses all five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
Then the five sense faculties should be able to apprehend it.
Internal phenomena consist of the four objects;
thus, the four [internal] faculties should be understood.
Furthermore, if the jar within the clay of internal phenomena were merely provisional, it should be perceivable by thought and mind;
yet this is not the case. Therefore, one knows that it does not exist.
The first half of the fourth verse reiterates the absence [of the object],
while the second half provides the actual refutation.
This refutation contains three points of meaning.
If both the characteristic and its concomitant were non-existent, then the cause would be identical to a non-cause;
the characteristic and its concomitant would not arise.
Furthermore, if both were non-causes, then there would be no cause at all.
Because the cause does not exist, that which is not the cause also does not exist.
Second, since both the characteristic and [the cause] are simultaneously non-existent, that which is not the cause is identical to the cause;
since both the characteristic and [the cause] are causes, there is nothing that is not a cause.
Since there is neither that which is non-cause nor that which is cause,
as for the third case— where both are non-existent yet there is both cause and non-cause—
it should likewise follow that both are causes, and thus existence and non-existence would both exist.
Furthermore, since they are equally non-existent, one would likewise have to seek fire in ice and milk in water;
thus, the relationship between cause and effect would be utterly disordered.
Question: Regarding the cause producing the effect, the second section refutes the pair of "giving the fruit" and "not giving the fruit."
First, the position that the cause acts as a cause for the effect was refuted;
next, the position that the cause does not act as a cause for the effect was refuted.
Thus, the initial thesis was established and subsequently demolished.
To establish the distinction between those within and without [the system], there are two gates concerning presence and absence in the prior [cause].
Because the cause acts as the cause for the fruit, it is not the case that the fruit is entirely absent within the cause;
yet, because the cause perishes immediately upon reaching its culmination, one cannot say that the fruit exists within the cause.
The masters of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* say:
"As a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*), the cause has two meanings.
The first is the cessation of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nirodha*)."
Second is transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Because the nature ceases, the cause ceases and the effect arises;
by way of the meaning of transformation, the cause is transformed into the effect.
Furthermore, it is said:
because the power of a single thought-moment as cause is sufficient to determine its fruit,
it is able to produce that fruit.
Because they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
they arise and then perish;
this is also the meaning of this [teaching].
Because the power to induce the fruition is sufficient, it is termed "giving the fruit.
The meaning of the cessation of its intrinsic nature is designated as "cessation.
Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states:
This cause acts as a cause for the fruit;
once the retribution has ceased, it persists into a subsequent birth.
Furthermore, it is said:
Although the causal agent has already ceased, its power remains established;
therefore, it is able to induce a result.
This is also the meaning of this principle.
The first half of the verse restates [the opponent's position] and the second half refutes it.
First, let us inquire into the meaning of the transformation of a prior nature through cessation:
if you maintain that there is only a single causal factor of milk, then if that milk were to cease, there would be nothing remaining to be transformed into curd.
If one says that milk transforms into the result of curd, then it cannot be said that the milk ceases.
Now, if one further claims that it both transforms and then ceases, then milk would possess two entities:
one entity would cease beforehand, [and another would remain].
The substance of the two milks transforms into curd;
originally, only one milk was established—
how can there be two?
He asked again:
"Regarding cause and effect, if the effect already exists, what need is there for a cause?
And if it does not exist, to whom would the cause act as a cause?"
Jiū says: Because there is the principle of having a fruit, it acts as the cause for the fruit.
If the principle were different from emptiness, then it would not need to act as such.
If it were not different from emptiness, then nothing could be given.
Furthermore, regarding your thesis, there are three possibilities: existence, non-existence, or both existence and non-existence.
As stated in the *Śata-śāstra*: "If it were to exist, it would be existent; if it were to be non-existent, it would be non-existent."
Furthermore, it challenges the interpretation of the Kaishan school, stating:
"There is that which is accomplished in the present,
and there is also that which arises in the present."
Regarding the accomplishment of the present [defilements], are they able to take an object or not?
If they are able to take an object, then being presently active, they would not be termed "accomplished.
If they are unable to take an object, this is identical to the position of the Vībhajyavādins regarding the dissociated latent dispositions (*viprayukta-anuśaya*).
Furthermore, Kaishan’s interpretation also represents the meaning of "the past of the past.
The initial moment's passing away constitutes one past;
having been accomplished in the present and having yielded its fruit, it then ceases.
Furthermore, this "one" is past;
it has already been lost and is lost again, just like the Kāśyapīyas.
Moreover, if you claim that this "one" exists as both ceasing and not ceasing, then it would possess two distinct natures.
First is the cause arising in the present;
second is the cause that brings about the future and the present.
Therefore, these are two distinct entities.
If one says that there is only a single entity that passes through two times, then time is merely a provisional designation for dharmas.
Since there are two times, there must be two dharmas;
consequently, there would be two causes and two effects.
He asked again: "If,
once the fruit has been attained, there is no longer any further accomplishment,
then one should also not say that the fruit, once attained, is called 'past'."
If that which has already passed is still called "past," then likewise, that which has already received its retribution should still be called "accomplished.
Question: If you claim that the cause does not descend [to produce] the fruit...
Second, [the opponent] refutes that the cause does not act as a cause for the effect.
Avoiding the two previous positions,
the outsider merely establishes that the cause ceases while the effect arises.
In the response, the first half restates [the opponent's position] while the second half refutes it.
The intent of the refutation is as follows:
prior to the cessation of the cause and before the existence of the effect, there would be no cause.
How could the fruit arise?
If the fruit were to arise, it would be a fruit without a cause.
Furthermore, the preceding verse clarifies that once the fruit has arisen, it ceases.
In that case, there would be the fallacy of having two causes.
Now, if it is clarified that the effect arises after the cause has already ceased,
then there is the fault of having no cause.
The former refutes the meaning of the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra);
the latter refutes the meaning of the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā).
Furthermore, the former also refutes the Mahāsāṃghika school.
Later, he refuted the doctrines of the Sthavira school.
Upon arriving in Chang’an, he observed that the masters of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* established two positions:
first, they maintained that the perfuming of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) is not extinguished and constitutes the retributive Buddha (*vipākabuddha*).
Second, establishing that the perfuming of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) is extinguished and does not constitute a *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha:
to say that it constitutes a Buddha would entail the fault of dual substantiality (*dvaita-doṣa*).
First, [the alternative is] that the perfuming of hearing transforms into a *vipākaphala-kāya* Buddha.
This is the sense of taking the impermanent to be permanent.
Second, the permeation of hearing is conditioned and,
furthermore, has the nature of cessation.
Therefore, the single perfuming of hearing falls into two categories.

Next, regarding the establishment of cessation: all meritorious qualities arise from the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*), whereas the perfuming of hearing arises merely as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
In reality, it does not produce a response from the Buddha;
therefore, it ceases.
It is like a craftsman who, using gold ore, merely creates the conditions for gold to emerge.
Yet gold emerges from its ore;
this is the meaning of the destruction of the cause.
Furthermore, this is the fundamental tenet held by the Satyasiddhi masters.
The adamantine mind has two meanings:
first, the cessation of the nature of real dharmas;
second, the sense of continuing in succession to become a Buddha.
Now, the position that the perfuming of hearing is not extinguished belongs exclusively to the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi) school.
It is asked: when the various conditions converge, the following third pair refutes [the notion of arising] both simultaneously and sequentially.
The first verse refutes simultaneity.
The intent of the question is as follows:
Since the fruit arises precisely when the various conditions converge,
there is no fault of [the fruit] being causeless.
This is also the Sarvāstivāda (Sa-po-to) position that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) constitute a person simultaneously,
and that the eight characteristics (*aṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*) arise together at once;
furthermore, it is the view of the Sāṃkhya school that cause and effect already exist in the future.
This is precisely "at one time.
It simply arises in the present;
it is merely that the cause precedes and the effect follows.
The answer states: "The first half of each line restates [the opponent's position], while the second half refutes it.
The intent of the refutation is as follows:
"In the principle of mutual production, that which is capable of producing is considered 'existent'."
Therefore, it is able to produce another;
since that which is produced would be non-existent, it is produced from another.
If one posits that they exist at the same time, then they must both exist together;
if they do not exist, they must both be non-existent.
If they are both non-existent, then that which is produced would merely be so, while that which produces it would lose its status as a producer.
If they were co-existent, then the producer would merely exist while the produced would be absent;
thus, if they were simultaneous, the relationship of producer and produced would be lost.
To possess the relationship of producer and produced, one must forfeit simultaneity.

Regarding the refutation of the conventional meaning: since you hold that the person and the aggregates exist simultaneously, why do you not say that the person is the cause and the limit of the aggregates is the fruit?
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
The name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) of sentient beings are bound to one another;
they should mutually act as causes and mutually serve as the substance [of one another].
Furthermore, these two dharmas exist simultaneously.
Apart from phenomena (dharma), there is no separate time.
If time is one, then phenomena are one;
if phenomena are two, then time is two.
If at the time when one dharma [exists], two should also exist; and if at the time when two dharmas [exist], one should also exist.
Furthermore, others say:
"The time when the cause ceases is the time when the effect arises."
If it exists when arising, it does not exist when ceasing;
how then could they be simultaneous?
Furthermore, regarding the statement that cause and effect are simultaneous: [this is untenable].
It may also possess both simultaneity and sequence. As stated in the *Póshù yì* (The Refutation of the Meaning of Number):
"Time is a provisional designation for dharmas that serve as causes."
If nine dharmas arise together, there would be nine moments.
If one says they arise at one and the same time, they should likewise arise as one and the same dharma.
Cause and effect cannot be a single dharma, nor can cause and effect be simultaneous.
Question: From the point where it was previously asked, "If the fruit exists first," down to this point, there are generally three meanings.
The first two pairs refute the prior cause and subsequent fruit;
the next section refutes the simultaneity of cause and fruit.
Now, the prior effect and the subsequent cause are refuted.
These three meanings encompass everything.
First they are established, and then they are refuted.
Both the sūtras and their commentaries contain this interpretation:
for example, although Sudatta had not yet cultivated the causes for building a vihāra,
he nonetheless experienced the fruit of rebirth in heaven.
Nanda has not yet actually committed an offense,
yet he already experiences the retribution of suffering and pleasure;
is this not a case of the effect preceding the cause?
Furthermore, Master Ying said:
"To first discard the walls and later prepare the pillars and beams" is also this same principle.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"The fruit of nirvana exists inherently from the beginning,
and one subsequently practices in order to attain it."
The answer states: "The first half restates [the opponent's position], while the second half refutes it.
The intent of the refutation is as follows:
originally, the effect exists by virtue of the cause."
If the cause does not yet exist, how can there be an effect?
If the effect were already present while the cause did not yet exist,
it would be called an effect without a cause.
Question: Since this was explicitly stated in the Sūtra, why do you refute it?
Should one not refrain from refuting the Sūtra in your treatise?
Answer: The sūtra’s statement that there are distinct [beings] has a profound underlying meaning.
It recounts the story of Sudatta in order to encourage people to cultivate merit;
it recounts the story of Nanda in order to warn against evil and exhort toward goodness.
It is only in contrast to the beginning of birth and death that there is this impermanence;
therefore, it is said that nirvāṇa is originally existent and permanent.
Nirvāṇa has never been either permanent or impermanent.
How could there ever be the two states of "original existence" (*mūlabhava*) and "initial existence" (*upapattibhava*)?
Furthermore, it is like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of a person being born alone at first,
followed by the application of one of the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) to moisten that birth, thereby making it firm for the duration of a single lifetime.
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is the primary sovereign of fruition;
it pervades the six destinies and the three realms.
Now, I ask:
From what does the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) arise?
Answer: It arises due to karma.
Question: If that is so, then the cause precedes and the effect follows.
Furthermore, if the fruit of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) were to arise after the prior cause has already ceased,
then there would be a fruit without a cause.
Moreover, if the afflictions (kleśa) were to arise later to moisten what already exists as a fruit, this would constitute a perverted moistening.
Furthermore, since the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth already exist,
why is it necessary for them to be moistened by any one of the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*)?
Moreover, if the effect precedes the cause, then the effect would arise from that which has not yet come into being.
The sequence of cause and effect is inverted and confused.
The question asks: "When the cause ceases, it transforms into the fruit.
Below this, the fourth section presents a pair of propositions: "the cause ceases and transforms" versus "the cause ceases but does not transform."
The thesis states: "That which undergoes transformation upon the cessation of the cause becomes the effect.
This is because, when examining the opponent's position, they merely designate 'cessation' itself as 'transformation.'
Therefore, the cause transforms into the effect immediately upon its cessation.
In the response, the first half refutes [the position] by showing that the cause reaches the effect; the second half refutes it by showing that [the effect] would have to be produced again.
The first phrase restates the position, and the second phrase refutes it.
The refutation states:
"Since the cause transforms to become the effect..."
Thus, the substance of the cause does not perish;
because the substance of the cause does not perish, the cause reaches the fruit.
Regarding the refutation of the second half [of the verse], which concerns the arising of the effect:
At the time of being the cause, it is one birth;
at the time of reaching the fruit, it is again one birth.
Therefore, this constitutes a double birth.
This merely causes a single entity to be born again,
which constitutes a logical fallacy.
Furthermore, it refutes the opponent's position as follows:
If the cause transforms to become the effect, then the effect would not differ from the cause;
it would simply be the prior cause acting as the subsequent effect.
It is like a person stretching a bow in the east who, upon reaching the west, remains still that same person stretching the bow.
If the cause were different from the effect, then the cause would perish before [producing] it;
thus, the cause would not produce the effect.
Again, he asked:
If the cause undergoes transformation to become the effect, then the cause would be different from the effect;
if it were not different, it should not undergo transformation.
It is also like the transformation of the former Deer King into a Buddha.
The Buddha must be the deer;
if he were not the deer, then the fruit would differ from its cause.
In that case, prior to the cessation of the cause and before the appearance of the fruit, there would be no cause at all.
"How can there be a fruit from that which has no cause?
He asked again,
"Does it arise through cessation and transformation, or without cessation and transformation?"
If it has ceased, there is nothing that can undergo transformation;
if it has not ceased, it does not transform.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that "what has already arisen arises again," as the Kai-shan school says:
At the time of acting as a cause, it constitutes one birth;
later, when it arises in the present through its accomplishment, it again constitutes one birth.
Thus, it falls into the fallacy of double birth.
The long exposition consists of two parts:
first, the explanation of the verses; second, the refutation of divergent views.
Regarding the "antecedent cause" (*pūrvaja-hetu*) and the "co-existent cause" (*sahabhū-hetu*): the antecedent cause refers to the causal relationship in which one thing gives rise to another.
Because the cause exists in a prior birth and the fruit exists in a subsequent birth,
it is called a "prior-birth cause.
As for the "simultaneous cause," it refers to the causal relationship between mutually dependent phenomena.
For example, when beams and pillars exist simultaneously with a house,
they are called co-arising causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
These two types of causes encompass all [causes].
Furthermore, to examine the characteristics of the arising of phenomena, there are inherently two types of cause and effect:
first, simultaneous causality, such as the growth of a tree;
second, sequential causality, such as the relationship between a retributive cause and its fruit.
Now, because one wishes to refute the cause that arises prior [to the effect], co-arising causes are excluded.
This clarifies that a prior-arising cause falls into the error of arising again.
Question: Why is the first half-verse not explained?
Answer: That the cause reaches the fruit is still an externalist position;
therefore, it need not be further explained.
If one claims that the cause itself transforms, this is refuted below in the second section, which refutes the doctrine of difference.
In all cases of refuting two positions,
the first refutation immediately undergoes a transformation.
An external defense states:
The cause thus transforms into the effect;
there is only a single arising and no repeated arising.
Therefore, it is now refuted as follows:
Since it is said that they are identical, one cannot call them changing;
if it is said that they are changing, one cannot call them identical.
It is like the eye being identical to the organ of sight—it cannot be called changing.
Question: Regarding the statement "the cause is not entirely extinguished," the second rebuttal below states:
"The name is extinguished, but the substance eternally persists;
because the substance persists, although there is transformation, there is identity."
Because the name has ceased, although they are identical, there is transformation.
Another says:
"The Deer King of former days was my own body."
The divine spirit of the deer and the divine spirit of the Buddha are not different;
it is only that the name "deer" ceases and the name "Buddha" arises.
The divine spirit of humans and devas is likewise not different.
It is merely that names perish and names arise.
Furthermore, according to the meaning of the Mahāsāṃghika school, the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure; it is neither cause nor fruit.
While in the state of a cause, it is called the "cause," yet from beginning to end it is one and the same mind.
Therefore, it is said that their substance is one;
yet when names differ, names are lost and names arise.
Furthermore, it is like the non-Buddhists [who proceed] from the subtle to the coarse.
The principle from the coarse to the subtle is likewise.
Furthermore, the masters of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* say:
"The essence of the ālayavijñāna is without arising or ceasing; it is its activity that is said to arise and cease."
This is also the meaning of this [passage].
Furthermore, this meaning contradicts the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*,
which clarifies the eight proofs for the meaning of cessation (*nirodha*).

The answer is: If one says that the lump of clay ceases first and the jar arises later, yet this is not called "transformation," it is because the name designates the substance and the substance corresponds to the name;
since the name has ceased, the substance likewise ceases.
If this is so, then how could the cessation of the former and the arising of the latter not constitute change?
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the lump of clay does not arise alone," this sentence clarifies that it is not only the name that arises, but the substance itself also arises.
Regarding the preceding phrase, not only is the designation extinguished, but the substance itself is also extinguished.
Furthermore, there are two points regarding the opponent:
first, that the substance of the cause is not extinguished.
Second is the view that the effect exists within the cause.
Previously, the non-extinction of the substance was refuted;
now, its existence is refuted.
Furthermore, this refutes the notion that the substance of clay is fixed and indestructible;
since two distinct things are joined, the substance is not fixed.
If it were merely a name, then this phrase says:
If you say that there is only the cessation of a name and the arising of a name,
then there would be only names;
since there would be no substance, what could it be that undergoes transformation?
Regarding the statement "the transformation of names is like milk transforming into curd":
this sentence proves that when a name ceases, its substance also ceases; and when a name arises, its substance also arises.
As the *Śata-śāstra* explains, because the five factors—form, time, power, name, and so forth—are distinct, they all cease together and arise together.
Refuting the opponent's position, he says: "If,
while as a single lump of clay it has not yet become a jar, it already possesses all the properties of a jar,
then your claim that when the clay becomes a jar, other properties do not undergo cessation through non-apprehension (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is untenable."
One might also ask: "Is there not also the principle of the differentiation of jars, whereby a jar is established?
The answer is: "There is indeed the principle of the differentiation of jars.
For example, when a single lump of clay is used to produce one object, all other objects [made from that same clay] are thereby differentiated."
Question: Since they cannot be accomplished simultaneously, nor can they be differentiated simultaneously, how is it so?
Answer: The accomplishment of things occurs through a single event.
Because it is difficult, they cannot be established simultaneously.
Question: Since all principles exist concurrently, the phenomena must also exist concurrently.
Answer: Because the characteristics of phenomena obstruct one another, they cannot exist simultaneously.
Because principles do not obstruct one another, they can exist simultaneously.
Question: If there is the existence of principle and the existence of phenomena, then principle should obstruct principle and phenomena should obstruct phenomena.
If principle does not obstruct principle, then principle also does not exist.

Question: Although the cause has perished, [the effect] subsequently undergoes transformation; since it first perishes and then transforms, it falls into the error of two births. Second, the refutation of the non-transformation of destruction.
Therefore, it is now said:
"Because the cause perishes first and the effect arises later, there is no fault of [the effect] arising again.
In the response, the first half refutes the loss of the cause.
If there were no cause, what could produce an effect?
The second half of the verse clarifies that the cause is not lost;
since the cause already exists within the effect, how could it produce the effect?
Just as when rice is lost, there is nothing that can be made into cooked rice;
yet when it is not lost, even though the rice remains, there is still no cooked rice.
This is why he repeatedly refutes the notion that it is "not lost."
The opponent establishes that cause and effect consist only of two possibilities: either loss or non-loss.
If one refutes non-loss, then loss is established;
if one refutes loss, then non-loss is established.
Therefore, it is refuted by advancing and retreating.
Question: How does this differ from the refutation in the preceding verse?
Answer: The former refutes [the notion of] being born again.
Now, by gathering [these factors], they are prevented from arising.
Furthermore, as in the *Abhidharmakośa* and other treatises, within a single meaning there exist both loss and non-loss;
in the case of substantial dharmas (*dravyadharma*), there is loss.
Because the continuity is not lost,
[the opponent] refutes it in its entirety.
If real dharmas were lost, then there would be no cause for the production of an effect.
If the continuity is not lost, then the cause must exist within the fruit.
Furthermore, this passage elucidates the meaning of "response" (感) and "inducement" (應). Now, I ask:
Regarding that which is to be produced through a wholesome cause: is this wholesome [action] existent or non-existent?
If it is existent, what need is there for it to produce [a result]?
If you claim that the principle is good because it evokes a response and the phenomenon accordingly accords with it,
then the principle would be the cause that evokes and the phenomenon the result;
thus, according to your doctrine, there would be nothing other than sentient beings.
If sentient beings exist, then all principles of goodness exist.
Since all sentient beings are constantly able to evoke the sages,
there would be no need to cultivate specific good deeds in order to evoke specific worldly fruits.
He asked again:
"If there is that which is good when not yet present but should already be present,
should there also be that which is present when not yet present but should already be good?"
He asked again regarding the meaning of "inducing":
"If that which has not yet occurred cannot induce a fruit,
then it should also follow that wholesome states which have not yet occurred cannot induce the state of an Arya."
He asked again:
"Regarding your meaning of 'response and resonance' (yinggan), why are they not mutually corresponding?
According to principle, the stimulus (ji) should correspond to the phenomenon (shi), and the phenomenon should correspond to the stimulus."
Just as principle responds to the stimulus of phenomena,
phenomena should likewise respond to the stimulus of principle.
Next, the question was asked:
Regarding that which is well capable of producing results in the two periods of past and present:
since it already exists within the wholesome,
why would it need to produce [a result]?
If you say that it is experienced for the purpose of increasing and producing wholesome states,
then if such wholesome states do not yet exist, they should not be experienced;
how, then, could the first moment of a wholesome state arise?
If a single moment of wholesome thought arises spontaneously without requiring the response of a sage,
then later moments should likewise arise spontaneously without requiring such a response.
Furthermore, he asked about adornment.
Since both [the past and future] existents are thus without intrinsic reality, how can the past be established?
If the past is established, how can you say it does not exist?
If past causes were to induce future effects,
then past understanding should also sever future afflictions; yet,
if those afflictions do not exist, they cannot be severed.
Furthermore, it should follow that the fruit cannot fail to be induced.
Again, he asked about the meaning of "attainment" according to Guangzhai.
The Sūtra says:
Conditioned phenomena are impermanent,
yet you claim that the arising of a single thought of good or evil is a constant function;
does this not contradict the sutras?
Furthermore, there is the fallacy that within the impermanent there would be the permanent, and within the permanent there would be the impermanent.
The question asks: "Is this cause pervasive? This introduces the fifth pair of propositions concerning whether the effect is pervasive or non-pervasive.
In calculating cause and effect, each perspective differs:
seeing a seed within the lotus, one concludes it existed previously;
seeing that it arises only upon depending on conditions, one concludes it did not exist previously.
To see that the cause ceases as the effect arises is to say that the cause precedes the effect;
yet, to maintain that it still acts as the cause for the effect is to say that the cause follows the effect.
To see that the individual fingers come together to form a fist is to say that cause and effect exist simultaneously.
Seeing milk transform into curd, one says that the cause changes to become the effect.
Seeing an image within a mirror, one says that the cause perceives the effect.
Seeing the seed perish and the sprout arise, one says that the cause does not perceive the effect.
Seeing oil emerge from within sesame seeds, one says it exists everywhere;
yet seeing a mother give birth to a child, one says it does not exist everywhere,
for the child resides only within the womb and not throughout the four limbs.
Therefore, wishing now to exhaustively investigate all these arguments,
I shall refute them in their entirety.
This verse clarifies that if [the whole] were pervasive, it would be present in its full substance throughout.
What further thing is produced by this?
For example, when the five fingers are completely curled, what further thing is produced by that curling?
If they were not complete [in being curled], could you manage to curl them such that one finger is on one side and another finger is on the other side?
Furthermore, as for that which is rolled up but does not pervade the finger,
does it exist outside the finger, inside the finger, or in between?
Neither is established.
Whether it is seen or not seen is still a matter of being pervasive or non-pervasive;
and pervasiveness, too, would already exist within the cause.
"Not pervasive" means it was previously non-existent.
Because the entire substance is [the manifestation], it is called "pervasive";
because the entire substance is [the perception], it is called "seeing."
The prose [commentary] states that because [the effect] is already present within the cause, it does not need to arise;
it further states that because [the effect] is not seen to be absent within the cause, it cannot arise.
One should carefully examine the text to see this.
The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* say:
"Sentient beings possess the principle of being able to be born throughout all the various realms of the six destinies. The masters of the *Saṃghabhedavastu* (or *Śāriputrābhidharma*) say:
The future exists; it pervasively possesses the natures of the five destinies and the three vehicles.
Upon reaching the stage of *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*, two of the three vehicle-natures and all three evil destinies are non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Now I ask: in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is said that [the Buddha] refuted Srenika by saying,
"If the self were omnipresent throughout all realms of existence..."
For what reason would one create karma again for the sake of the body?
Since those who will exist in the future already universally possess bodies within the five destinies,
they too face this same difficulty.
He [the opponent] offers this defense:
"The future exists; however, its nature is different from the 'self' (ātman) of the non-Buddhists."
Now I ask:
this distinctness from emptiness is already existent;
if it has not yet become distinct from emptiness, what constitutes its nature?
He asked again:
"For what reason is there this nature of the future?
Therefore, we know that it exists inherently from the beginning."
This is the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, if one says that past causes [exist], this second section provides a general refutation of cause and effect.
Previously, there was a specific refutation of ten schools and five pairs.
Now, the general refutation consists of five pairs:
first, the refutation of the conjunction and non-conjunction;
second, the refutation of the empty and the non-empty.
1. Refutation of the identity of the three;
2. Refutation of existence and non-existence through the four natures; 3. Refutation of the incompatibility of conjunction.
The first four verses are divided into two parts:
the first three verses refute conjunction,
and the final verse refutes both conjunction and non-conjunction.
Regarding these three verses, there are exactly three [points],
all of which clarify that the causes of a single lifetime do not conjoin with the effects of the three time periods.
As for why they refute such conjunction:
Because the cause is able to produce the fruit, it is said that "the cause and the fruit conjoin.
Because the fruit is able to repay the cause, it is said that "the fruit and the cause conjoin.
Question: Regarding the refutation of the opponent's position, it says:
If a past cause can produce a present effect,
since the past has already ceased and is non-existent,
how could it be able to produce a present effect?
This refutes the meaning established by the adornment.
If that which was past were to transition into the present, it would no longer be called "past.
If it were to transition, it would follow that it is eternal.
"How can one constantly obtain retribution?
This refutes the interpretation of Kaishan.
Furthermore, if there were a past habitual cause capable of producing a present fruit, then since it is designated as "existing," it would be the present and could not be called the past.
This [explanation] generally refutes the various schools.
A question is raised:
"How can a cause in the future obtain a fruit in the future?"
He replied to him:
"One shall attain the principle of Buddhahood.
This principle resides in the future; once the body is purified, one shall attain bodhi."
Furthermore, one should cultivate the causes to attain bodhi;
furthermore, one should cultivate the causes to attain the future fruit.
It is also said:
All sentient beings constantly possess the principle of future arising as their potential;
the sages respond to this as its fruition—
this is the nature of these matters.
Question: How is it that a cause in the future can have its principle reside in the fruit?
Answer: It is like the present response of the Sage being triggered by the conditions of the future.
Question: How is it that a cause in the future can be the fruit of the past?
Answer: Because there is the principle that one will attain Buddhahood in the future, based on this cause, one severs afflictions and seeks Buddhahood throughout both the future and present periods.
Now, the question is asked:
If the future [cause] is already able to act as the cause for the abandonment of afflictions,
it should likewise follow that the future [cause] already possesses the capacity to abandon present delusions.
Furthermore, the same difficulty applies to the claim that a future fruit is already able to produce a present mind.
Question: How does a present fruit act as a cause for the past?
Answer: This is a "successive conventional cause" (*prabandha-prajñapti-hetu*).
It connects with the preceding cause so that the former is not severed, thereby acting as a cause for what follows.
If this is the case— that the present is caused by the past— how could the past not, in turn, arise from the present?
Again, he asked:
What is meant by "a future cause having a past result"?
Answer: According to common understanding, such a principle does not exist.
Now, this shall be clarified.
If the future serves as the cause for the past,
then the future is the cause and the past is the effect;
how then can the present be both cause and effect?
The Sūtra states:
"At the very moment this thought arose, the Buddha appeared in the air.
This manifestation is understandable in terms of its cause and its future fruit.
The present cause producing a past result is like practicing causes in the present to seek the originally existing Dharmakāya.
The prose section clarifies that the results of the three times do not coincide with the causes of the three times.
In the verse, the causes of the three times do not conjoin with the effects of the three times;
this is established through mutual refutation.
Furthermore, if there were no conjunction, the second verse would refute both conjunction and non-conjunction simultaneously.
The first half of the verse restates the previous argument that [causes and effects] do not combine, thereby clarifying that there is no production through combination.
The second half refutes the meaning of conjunction:
if the cause has already conjoined with the effect, there can be no further production through conjunction.
Thus, if the fruit already exists, it does not need to arise from its cause;
if the cause does not conjoin with the fruit,
this is the meaning of "no fruit."
There is nothing that cannot arise.
If [it is argued] that because the cause is empty there is no fruit, this is the second section, the refutation of emptiness by means of non-emptiness;
it consists of three verses divided into two parts.
The first verse refutes [the position] by means of whether the cause is empty or non-empty;
the following two verses refute it by means of whether the fruit is empty or non-empty.
This is still from the chapter on "Going and Coming," concerning the determined and the undetermined.
Furthermore, this refutation is directed at the chapter on the author [of the treatise] regarding whether they truly exist or truly do not exist;
it summarizes their essential points and thus this refutation was composed.
This is easy to see.
Regarding the point that cause and effect are one, the third section below refutes this through the gate of identity and difference.
The first verse both cites these two positions and denies them both.
The second verse presents a double citation and a double refutation.
First, there are four faults regarding [the position that] "there is": first, if there were only the cause, there would be no fruit.
There is neither fruit nor cause;
both are merely fruit without cause.
Without cause, there is also no fruit.
Third, since these are one and the same thing, they cannot be described as cause and effect.
Fourth, if cause and effect are one, then the agent and the action must also be one;
the potter and the jar would be identical.
Difference also involves four difficulties.
First, if the cause differs from the effect and also differs from what is not a cause,
then both would equally be non-causes.
Second, both cause and non-cause together constitute a cause.
Third, when a cause constitutes a non-cause, that non-cause constitutes a cause.
Fourth, where there is a cause and a non-cause, there is then both difference and non-difference.
If the effect were definitely existent by nature, this would be refuted in the fourth section below regarding the existence or non-existence of that nature.
The first verse clarifies that an existent or non-existent effect cannot be produced by a cause.

That which possesses intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is an existent entity (vastu). For example, if a person existed inherently, their human body would not need to be constituted by the aggregates (skandha);
if a person did not exist inherently, the combination of the aggregates could not constitute them.
The second verse concludes that there is no cause-and-effect.

If, according to the fifth [verse], a result cannot arise from a combination of various causes and conditions due to the union or non-union of conditions, then how can it be said that a result arises from a combination, as the first verse explicitly clarifies? It states that arising from a combination is impossible; how, then, could it produce a result?
Because the cause does not exist, the effect does not exist.
The second verse combines these points to establish the meaning of non-arising through the absence of both conjunction and disjunction.
Because the effect does not exist, the cause does not exist.
Therefore, it is said: "Where could there be a combination of dharmas?
These two verses have the same meaning as the two verses at the end of the *Pratyaya-parivarta*.
The prose commentary merely explains these two verses from the fifth section.
The first two [sections] are easy to understand, so they are not explained here in detail.
Chapter Twenty-one: On Formation and Destruction (Nine-fascicle Edition). This chapter contains six points of meaning.
First, from the beginning of the treatise to its conclusion,
twenty sections in total have been completed to seek the person and phenomena within cause and effect, yet neither is found.
Thereupon, the opponent says:
If the fundamental establishment of all phenomena were subject to refutation, they would be destroyed;
since there is both establishment and destruction, the myriad transformations are not empty.
Second, the opponent establishes the worldly dharmas across twenty chapters.
Previously, the worldly dharmas were established separately with twenty sections;
now, they are collectively established as worldly dharmas that are all characterized by impermanence and decay.
Thus, one knows that there is a world.
Thus, whereas previously [the arguments] were established and refuted individually,
they are now established and refuted collectively;
for this reason, there is this chapter.
Third, if all the various schools—great and small, internal and external—are refuted, then the meaning of Nāgārjuna is established.
If this is so, it does not follow that the myriad phenomena (*dharmas*) do not exist.
Fourth, cause and effect are the fundamental tenet of all these meanings.
Once it is refuted, the principle of cause and effect collapses.
If there is collapse, there must be establishment; therefore, this chapter exists.
Fifth, while the preceding chapters have primarily refuted internal [Buddhist] doctrines,
this chapter refutes external [non-Buddhist] doctrines,
just as one explains the formation and destruction of heaven and earth.
Now I clarify:
the world was originally unformed and now likewise does not perish.
My Pure Land is indestructible, yet the multitudes see it as being utterly consumed by fire.
This is such that those who see formation perceive formation, while those who see disintegration perceive disintegration;
it is like two conditions perceiving a single substance as either pure or impure,
yet all phenomena have never actually undergone formation or disintegration.

Sixth, those among the world’s non-Buddhists and followers of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna hear that within the sūtras it is taught that the five-wheel world-systems are formed and the three calamities destroy them;
and that when the five aggregates combine to form sentient beings, their dispersal constitutes the destruction of sentient beings.
Even down to the direct observation of the formation and destruction of jars and garments, and the formation and destruction of human birth and death—
because one has already seen such formation and destruction, afflictions of craving and views, as well as karma and suffering, arise, and one fails to attain liberation.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take pity on these sentient beings;
they clearly know that such formation and destruction do not truly exist.
Therefore, the subsequent text says:
If one claims that arising and ceasing exist because they are perceived through direct observation, that is merely delusion and falsehood.
Since the objects perceived do not exist,
the perceiving mind is likewise as described.
That which is called "non-existent" means there are no objects externally;
that which is called "non-being" means there is no mind internally.
When internal and external are simultaneously darkened, both object and contemplation are tranquil.
This is called nirvana;
thus, one attains liberation.
For these reasons, this chapter is taught.
Question: What is meant by "formation" and "dissolution"?
Answer: Formation refers to the convergence of various conditions;
dissolution refers to the dispersal of those various conditions.
Briefly stated, there are four meanings.
First, it refers to phenomena before one's eyes:
when things aggregate, they form; when they disperse, they perish.
Second, the two characteristics of arising and abiding constitute formation,
while the two characteristics of change and cessation constitute destruction.
Third, the conjunction of the five wheels constitutes the formation of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
When the three calamities arise during the kalpa of destruction, the receptacle world (bhājanaloka) is destroyed;
when the six types [of beings] assemble, the sentient world (sattvaloka) is formed.
When the three minor kalpas arise, the sentient world is destroyed.
Fourth, in terms of their underlying principles: for example, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) subvert the Buddha-dharma;
the Abhidharmikas subvert the *hari* fruit;
and the various schools subvert Nāgārjuna.
Furthermore, those who follow the *Dilun* school employ the doctrine of the six characteristics (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*) to explain various sūtras—

namely, the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the identical characteristic (*tulyalakṣaṇa*), the different characteristic (*bhinnalakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of formation (*siddhilakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of disintegration (*bhaṅgalakṣaṇa*). Yet, when one seeks such formation and disintegration in their totality, they are ultimately unfindable.
To understand that all phenomena are fundamentally unestablished from the beginning and are likewise without disintegration is itself the Middle Way;
by giving rise to contemplation within this causal state, conceptual proliferation is extinguished.
Therefore, it is categorized by way of its characteristics. This category is divided into eight sections:
first, the section on commonality and separation.
1. The gate of clarifying the absence of formation and destruction;
2. The gate of the exhausted and the inexhaustible;
3. The gate of essence and characteristics.
4. The gate of emptiness and non-emptiness;
5. The gate of identity and difference;
6. The gate of arising and ceasing.
The seventh is the gate of severing permanence and annihilation;
the eighth is the gate of the three periods of time.
Regarding the first, there are three [subsections].
First, the two gates are jointly distinguished;
second, the two gates are jointly explained;
third, the two gates are jointly concluded.
Initially, the opponent asks only regarding the "worldly" (loka).
Since this chapter refutes worldly phenomena across twenty-one sections and concludes with them,
the opponent specifically inquires about the world.
Furthermore, because the impermanent phenomena of the world undergo formation and destruction,
he specifically asks about the world that currently manifests signs of decay and ruin.
In the preceding twenty chapters, there is no doubt raised by the Master that he has not refuted,
nor is there any argument advanced by outsiders that he has not defeated;
therefore, it is said that these manifest signs of ruin have appeared.
Furthermore, from the preceding sections up to this point, the thesis was established by way of the door of establishment (*siddhi-mukha*);
now, in this chapter, the thesis is established by way of the door of destruction (*bhaṅga-mukha*).
Since we currently perceive that the entities of the self (*ātman*) and the aggregates (*skandha*) are all subject to destruction, they must necessarily have been previously established.
In the response, the first half [of the verse] clarifies that there is no destruction by opening two gates: the gate of conjunction and the gate of separation.
The reason why non-destruction was clarified previously is that the opponent claimed their own doctrine would be destroyed; therefore, it was examined first.
The latter half, concerning the non-establishment of both [arising and ceasing],
is easily understood.
Next, three verses explain the absence of arising and ceasing.
This is divided into three distinct sections.
The first verse explains the gate of "being devoid of formation and thus being indestructible.
The third verse explains the gate of "being devoid of destruction and thus being without formation."
The intermediate verse explains the gate of neither formation nor destruction together with both formation and destruction.
Since these two are mutually distinct, they are explained separately;
since they function together, they are explained collectively.
This is also easily understood.
Question: For what reason does the text cite birth and death to refute the opponent?
Answer: "External" refers to the opponent’s own position, which is the argument of death; "internal" refers to the Master [Nāgārjuna], who is the argument of life.
Therefore, even when refuting [this view], we do not allow for death from the outside.
You have only just attained birth above; you may now die.
But since you have never actually been born, how can you die now?
One may say:
"Seeking life, one cannot find it;
seeking death, likewise one cannot find it."
Regarding the statement that "impermanence has never existed nor does it abide at any time within phenomena":
according to the opponent, since the four characteristics are always co-present, once there is arising and abiding,
change and cessation must necessarily follow.
Above, it was shown that there is no formation or destruction based on the coarse death and birth of the macroscopic period;
now, it is clarified that there is likewise no formation or destruction in the subtle arising and ceasing of every moment.
Furthermore, this also refutes both these coarse and subtle types of arising and ceasing.
The prose commentary explains [the text] in accordance with the sequence of the verses in the preceding chapter,
rather than following the latter three verses. First,
it explains that the two gates of "commonality" and "separation" are indestructible.

If [the entity] were separate [from its parts], it would be destroyed; if it were both together and separate, it would likewise be destroyed. Next, the following explains that neither the "together" nor the "separate" model is established.
This is divided into two sections. First, regarding the explanation of the failure of the "separate" model to establish [the entity], there are three points.
This refers to the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion.
Within the explanation, there are generally two refutations;
the first is the refutation by way of [showing] the absence of a cause.
Furthermore, following the refutation of the established dharma, we shall next perform the refutation by means of the absence of a result.
Since the destruction of this established result constitutes the cause of destruction,
and there is thus no cause for its establishment.
Therefore, there is no destruction of the fruit.
Thus ends the third section below.
The refutation of the shared position that there is destruction also consists of three parts.
This refers to the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion. Within the explanation, it says:
"The phenomena are established separately first, and subsequently there is their conjunction."
If arising were coexistent with destruction, then there would be both arising and destruction;
if destruction were coexistent with arising, then there would be both destruction and arising. Because there is both destruction and arising, there is no arising.
Where there is no formation, there is no destruction.
If you now wish to bring them together,
it must first be that both entities are individually formed before they can then be joined.
Therefore, it is said that the phenomena are established prior to their conjunction.
Since you cannot establish two distinct entities independently,
how can they be conjoined?
Regarding "legitimate non-separation": even if one allows for their distinctness to be established, when two things are conjoined, they remain distinct despite the conjunction;
just as two pieces of wood, though joined together, ultimately remain distinct from one another.
If it were ultimately distinct from itself, then it would not be a unity.
If "destruction through separation" implies that destruction occurs without a cause,
then "separation" is simply the absence of difference.
Even if formation and destruction were combined such that their essences were not distinct, then destruction would immediately destroy formation;
thus, there would be no formation.
What, then, could serve as the cause of destruction?
Therefore, it is said that there is no cause.
Thus, if they are different, there would be a cause but no union;
if they are not different, there is union but no cause.
Therefore, this concludes the third section below.
If one were to separate [the two], the second explanation—that neither of the two doors of "separation" nor "non-separation" can establish the meaning—would fail.
First, both are cited together; next, both are explained together.
Those who analyze phenomena are the Abhidharmikas;
they maintain that the eight characteristics arise simultaneously with the substance of the phenomenon.
Thus, within the characteristics of arising and abiding, there are always the characteristics of change and cessation.
Therefore, we now refute this.
If there were constant arising and ceasing, then there would be no abiding;
thus, neither formation nor destruction could be established. This third single verse summarizes [the argument].
The first half of the verse provides a double conclusion, while the second half offers a refutation.
The first half states:
"Neither arising nor ceasing are established together. Here, "established" (*siddha*) refers to the establishment of a meaning.

Since the arguments for the formation and destruction of external objects are not established when examined through the two gates of "together" and "separately," it is said that "there is no formation.

The world is precisely the three realms of existence (*tribhava*).
Therefore, one must destroy these three realms of existence.
As for the "three," followers of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna perceive the arising of these three realms of existence.
And one desires to extinguish the three realms of existence (*tribhava*).
The Master of the Treatise says:
"If one perceives the arising and ceasing of the three realms of existence, then one cannot extinguish the three realms of existence."

Only when one realizes that the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātu*) are fundamentally unborn from the beginning and do not perish even now can one truly extinguish the three realms of existence. Furthermore,
the Abhidharma-piṭaka elucidates the four types of existence (*catasra upapattayaḥ*).

There are the existence at birth (*upapatti-bhava*), the existence at death (*maraṇa-bhava*), the intermediate existence (*antarā-bhava*), and the existence of the present life (*pūrvakāla-bhava*). Furthermore, there are two types of birth and death that constitute two kinds of existence:
namely, *paricchinna-vaiparītya* (fragmentary) and *pariṇāma-vaiparītya* (transformative).
Furthermore, the seven cycles of birth and death constitute the seven modes of existence (*bhava*).
Now, if one seeks such existences, they are simply unobtainable.
Since these births and deaths were originally unarisen, there is now nothing to be extinguished; thus, one attains liberation from the seven cycles of birth and death.
To see that there are seven cycles of birth, death, arising, and ceasing is not to be separate from those seven cycles of birth and death;
therefore, the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) are refuted.
Fourth, this is to manifest the Master’s intention in the twenty-one chapters of refuting worldly phenomena.
The reason for destroying worldly dharmas is to cause sentient beings to know that the world is ultimately empty,
so that they may awaken to the non-existence of the three realms of existence and attain liberation from them.
The four verses constitute four [refutations]:
the first refutes [the notion that] cessation is non-cessation;
the second refutes [the notion of] both existing simultaneously.
Third, the refutation by means of birth-and-death and existence;
fourth, the summary refutation.
The first half of the initial verse states:
If the prior existence were to cease, the subsequent existence would be without a cause.
According to the second half [of the verse], if the prior existence does not cease, then two existences would exist simultaneously.
If the prior existence were to cease, its cessation would mean it becomes non-existent.
If that which arises later does not exist because the initial existence has not ceased, then how could that later existence arise? It would be obstructed.
How, then, could it come into being?
Question: Regarding the second verse on "arising later," the first part of the question does not refute the two preceding [positions];
rather, it establishes one's own thesis precisely at the moment when [the other position] is extinguished.
In the response, the first half restates [the opponent's position] and the second half refutes it.
The intent of the refutation is as follows:
If the time when the prior existence ceases were the same as the time when the subsequent existence arises, then the two existences would exist simultaneously.
Your statement that arising occurs at the time of cessation implies that arising and cessation are simultaneous;
yet, the existence of birth is not the existence of death, which would mean there are two existences at one and the same time.
If two existences do not occur simultaneously, then one ceases while the other arises; it is not the case that arising occurs at the very moment of cessation.
[The opponent] asks: "This is the third refutation of the lower position. [The author] replies:
"In the preceding question, the 'two' were already refuted."
However, when confronted with this, the opponent is unable to provide a reasoned response;
since no answer can be given regarding whether [the birth] occurs before, after, or simultaneously, they merely say, "it is seen by the eye.
As for this "seeing by the eye," it means that if this person dies here, they are immediately reborn there.
In the response, the first half restates [the opponent's position] and the second half refutes it.
The intent of the refutation is as follows:
if you wish to maintain that at the time of cessation there are not two existences (*bhava*), then birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) would constitute a single existence.
This constitutes one aggregate (skandha) that both arises and dies.
If death were not immediately followed by birth, there would still be two existences:
first, the existence of the intermediate state (antarābhava), and second, the existence of the two aggregates of birth.
This death-aggregate gives rise to a birth-aggregate.
The fourth verse concludes the refutation.
The first half of the verse restates the preceding method of refutation.
When form arises from desire, desire comes first and form follows;
the same applies to the formless realm.
The second half [of the verse] refutes the externalist calculation that [things] exist.
Because outsiders do not realize that [existence] is non-existent, the three realms of existence (tridhātu) are not severed.
If one awakens to the fact that existence is non-existence, one can extinguish the three realms of existence;
this reveals the Master’s intention in refuting the three realms of existence.
